name: Build a PR media list from live coverage with Bright Data, GPT-5.6 and Google Docs

parameters.content:
## Build a media list from who is publishing on your subject, not from a database

Fill in a subject, one or two companies like yours, and your story in a line. You get back a ranked list of journalists with the piece each one published and an angle to open with, as a Google Doc.

### How it works

Two Bright Data news searches run side by side: one on your subject, one on your comparable companies. **`Find The Bylines`** merges them and counts, so an outlet that turns up in both lists outranks one that only covers the topic. That ordering is the reason for two searches.

The top articles are then read through the Web Unlocker as raw HTML, because a search result carries the outlet and not the reporter - the name sits in the page's `author` metadata, which a markdown conversion throws away. One model call ranks the shortlist against your story line and writes an opening angle for each name.

Every name carries why it is on the list: found on your subject, on companies like yours, or on both. The last group is the one to call first, and it is the only thing two searches can tell you that one cannot.

### Setup

1. Bright Data, as a Header Auth credential. The free tier is 5,000 credits a month with no card.

2. An OpenAI credential and a Google Docs credential.

3. Open the form URL, fill it in, and wait on the page. The finished list appears there and in your Drive.

## 1. A subject, and two companies like yours
Those two companies are the whole reason this beats a media database. Everything else is looked up.

## 2. Two searches, not one
One finds who covers the subject. The other finds who covers companies at your stage. A name in both is the call to make first.

## 3. Rank the pages before paying to read them
Wire services are your own industry's press releases coming back at you, so they are dropped by name before anything is counted.

## 4. The news tab will not give you an address
Every news link is a relative `/goto?url=...` redirect. Searching the exact headline again returns the same story with a real URL.

## 5. The name is in the head, not the prose
Read as raw HTML on purpose: markdown drops the document head, and the head is where `meta name="author"` lives.

## 6. One call, because ranking is a comparison
Eight separate calls would each be paying full price to rank a list of one.

## 7. A document and a page
The Docs insert writes the string it is handed, so the layout is built out of line breaks rather than markdown.

## A byline is a starting point, not a contact

This finds who wrote about your subject and where. It does not find their email, and it should not: scraping a journalist's inbox address to cold-pitch them is the behaviour that got PR databases their reputation.

Use the name and the piece to decide who is worth approaching, then approach them the way that outlet asks to be approached - the tips page, the public handle, or an introduction.

Some pages name no author anywhere in their markup. Those are kept as outlet-level rows rather than dropped, so the list will contain entries with a publication and no person. That is honest, not a gap.

The news tab is searched rather than the web, and then each headline is looked up again to get an address. That is not indirection for its own sake: news results come back as `/goto?url=...` redirects that cannot be fetched - ten of ten when measured - while a plain web search on the same subject returns vendor blog posts rather than journalism. Neither one alone gives you a media list.
